pages.title: Device and cable
pages.for: The device protects the cable, so it is chosen from Ib and the cable from the device, where the cable runs hottest: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz. The cable must also take the current that finally operates the device: I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz (Regulation 433.1.1; slides p.22, 32).
pages.rule:
Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, and I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz
It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × Ci × Cf), only the factors that act together
Iz = tabulated figure × the same factors, except Cf
BS 3036 fuse: Cf = 0.725 (1.45 ÷ 2)

Work It for each part of the run and design to the highest, on the reference method that cuts Iz most (slides p.25, 27, 28).
Cg counts the circuit itself; a cable at no more than 30% of its grouped rating may be left out (Table 4C1 note 9).
BS EN 60898 breakers, BS 88 fuses: I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz is met once Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz holds (Regulation 433.1.201).
A motor's thermal relay: In is its setting; check its own curve.

traps.text: Multiplying factors that never act together (24.18 A where 21.28 A is right), or designing to the easier section or reference method.
Leaving the circuit being installed out of Cg.
A rewireable fuse without Cf: its I2 can pass the cable's 1.45 Iz.
traps.cite: Slides p.25; Professional Electrician (NICEIC), in research

traps.text: Sizing a star-delta motor's six cables on the line current: they carry a winding's current.
traps.cite: Pack p.4 (delta running conditions); Schneider Electric and Siemens, in research

traps.text: Reading 90 °C ratings when the starter's or motor's terminals are designed for less: rate the cables at the terminals' temperature (at 70 °C, 1.5 mm² carries only 15.5 A).
traps.cite: Table 4E1A note 1; Table 4D1A column 5 (your copy p.448, 458)

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz: the device at least the design current, the cable where it runs at least the device; and the current that finally operates the device, I2, no more than 1.45 Iz.
pages.alt: REGULATION 433.1.1 · YOUR SLIDES P.22 Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz In ≥ Ib: the device's rating or current setting is at least the design current. Iz ≥ In: the cable's current-carrying capacity, where it is installed, is at least the device's. The table's figure, It, is for a single circuit at the table's ambient; Iz is what the cable carries continuously where it actually runs. I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz One more condition: the current that finally operates the device, I2, is no more than 1.45 Iz.
pages.html:
Regulation 433.1.1 · your slides p.22

Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz

In ≥ Ib: the device's rating or current setting is at least the design current.

Iz ≥ In: the cable's current-carrying capacity, where it is installed, is at least the device's.

The table's figure, It, is for a single circuit at the table's ambient; Iz is what the cable carries continuously where it actually runs.

I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz

One more condition: the current that finally operates the device, I2, is no more than 1.45 Iz.

If it is skipped or wrong: a cable carrying more than it can shed runs hot, and over time that damages insulation, joints, terminations and their surroundings.

pages.name: The why: the run in sections
pages.text: The trunking section sets the cable at 21.28 A; only where all three act in one place is it 24.18 A.
pages.alt: Your slides' heater circuit (p.26), In 16 A, drawn as its route in three sections. Clipped Ca 0.94 It 17.02 A Trunking Ca 0.94 Cg 0.8 It 21.28 A Insulated wall Ca 0.94 Ci 0.88 It 19.34 A Sets the cable In trunking with another circuit: the warm room and the grouping act together. 0.94 × 0.8 = 0.752 16 ÷ 0.752 = 21.28 A The trunking needs the most, 21.28 A: there the warm room starts the cable warmer and the other circuit stops it shedding its heat, so it sets the cable. The wall needs 19.34 A and the clipped part 17.02 A.
pages.html:
Your slides' heater circuit (p.26), In 16 A, drawn as its route in three sections.

In trunking with another circuit: the warm room and the grouping act together.

0.94 × 0.8 = 0.752

16 ÷ 0.752 = 21.28 A

The trunking needs the most, 21.28 A: there the warm room starts the cable warmer and the other circuit stops it shedding its heat, so it sets the cable. The wall needs 19.34 A and the clipped part 17.02 A.With insulation inside the trunking too, all three act in one place, so the trunking needs 24.18 A: the one place where multiplying all three is right.

Its reference method sets the column too: your slides count only two methods in this run, B in the trunking and C clipped direct, and design to B; the wall has no column of its own here (p.28).

Cg always counts the circuit being installed (your slides p.25).

A cable expected to carry not more than 30% of its grouped rating may be ignored when finding the factor for the rest of the group (Table 4C1 note 9).

0.725 is 1.45 ÷ 2: the breaker's 1.45 over the fuse's 2.

Breakers to BS EN 60898 and fuses to BS 88 meet I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz whenever Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz holds (Regulation 433.1.201), as the breaker here does. A rewireable fuse needs Cf, and a motor's thermal relay is checked on its maker's curve.

Your assignment ED4-01A: pack p.3, and question 4 on p.4.

Carried forward
(a)Motor's design current, Ib23.08 A
(b)Each winding, in delta13.33 A

Given: the standard ratings near it, 16, 20, 25 and 32 A (On-Site Guide p.145).

23.08 A ≤ 25 A, the smallest standard rating not below it (20 A is below)

The type. A motor takes much more current starting than running. A star-delta start draws roughly 2 to 2.7 times full-load current, against 6 to 8 times direct-on-line (a calculator site's table, not a standard). The course takes 2.7, a practice value: 2.7 × 23.08 = 62.32 A (the motor's maker gives the real figure).

Type B, 3 to 5 In: 75 to 125 A

Type C, 5 to 10 In: 125 to 250 A

Type D, 10 to 20 In: 250 to 500 A

Which type of breaker, for the practice start of 62.32 A?

Type C.

The On-Site Guide names type C for small motors (p.90). The course chooses it, its own assumption: clear of the start, with more room than B.

Then the overload. The course puts the starter's thermal relay in the delta circuit (its assumption), where it is set to 0.58 × the motor's full-load (nameplate) current (0.58 is 1 ÷ √3, rounded) and never higher than the phase current: 23.08 ÷ √3 = 13.33 A. That setting is the In of the starter-to-motor cables.

Given: the room at 20°C (pack p.3). Six 90 °C thermosetting singles run from the starter to the motor, sized on the delta running conditions (pack p.4), in one conduit on the consultation bay's wall, clear of insulation (the course's assumption: Ci and Cf are 1).

First: how many circuits do the six singles count as for Cg?

Two circuits.

In delta running all six carry winding current, and n singles count as n/3 circuits of three loaded conductors for three-phase circuits (Table 4C1 note 5; On-Site Guide p.170).

6 ÷ 3 = 2 circuits; Table 4C1 item 1, two circuits bunched and enclosed: Cg 0.80.

Ca, a practice value: Table 4B1 is for ambients other than 30 °C, and its first row, 25 °C, gives 1.02 for 90 °C thermosetting. The course takes 1.00 at 20 °C, which takes no credit for the cool room: read the real treatment from your copy of Table 4B1.

13.33 ÷ (1.00 × 0.80) = 16.66 A

A thermal relay is not one of the devices Regulation 433.1.201 lists (step 4), so its own curve is read from its maker: it must operate by 1.45 × 16.00 = 23.20 A.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: State a hazard of an overload current in a circuit, and explain how the design keeps a small overload from harming the cable.
pages.why: A model answer: An overload makes the circuit conductors run hotter than the temperature they were chosen for, and over time that damages the insulation, joints and terminations and what surrounds them; it can lead to fire. The design guards the cable first with Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, and then with I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz: the current that finally makes the device operate must not exceed 1.45 times the cable's current-carrying capacity, so a small overload that lasts until the device opens does not deteriorate the cable (your slides p.32). A rewireable fuse to BS 3036 can need up to about twice its rating to operate, so its rating is kept to 0.725 Iz, your slides' Cf (p.25).
